planting.note: Plant small corms shallowly in autumn into gritty, fast-draining soil so winter rains can trigger growth, then let foliage die back completely through the dry Cape summer dormancy.

directions: Geissorhiza aspera is a diminutive Western Cape corm that produces velvety, wiry stems topped with small star-shaped flowers in deep blue to violet, often with a darker central blotch, opening in late winter and early spring. It grows naturally on moist, sandy flats near Cape Agulhas and needs a sharply drained, sandy mix with ample winter moisture followed by a bone-dry summer rest to mimic its native Mediterranean-type climate. Because the corms and foliage are small, it is best massed in a bulb frame, raised bed, or shallow pot where its color can be appreciated up close. Avoid any summer irrigation once the foliage yellows, as rot in dormancy is the most common cause of loss in cultivation.

planting.note: Set out corms or divisions in spring into well-drained, fertile soil; established clumps resent disturbance so choose a permanent site.

directions: Watsonia knysnana is a tall, graceful bugle lily from forest-edge sandstone slopes in South Africa's Eastern Cape, forming erect fans of sword-shaped leaves that sheath the lower stem. From late spring into summer it sends up spikes of wide, funnel-shaped flowers in shades of pale pink to deep purplish-red, held above the foliage on sturdy stems well suited to cutting. It is closely related to Watsonia pillansii and can hybridize where the two overlap in the wild, so garden plants grown from seed may show some variation in flower color. Give it a sunny border with good drainage and consistent moisture during active growth, and mulch corms in winter in marginal zones since it is not reliably frost-hardy.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in a sheltered, south-facing spot with sharp drainage, since this species dislikes winter wet more than most other dieramas.

directions: Dierama igneum is a slow-growing wandflower endemic to the southeastern Cape provinces and southern KwaZulu-Natal, forming clumps of narrow, grasslike leaves beneath long, arching stems. Its trumpet-shaped flowers are normally salmon pink, dangling gracefully from the thin, wiry stem tips in summer much like its better-known relatives. It is hardy to around 14 degrees Fahrenheit, but because it dislikes winter moisture it performs best on a sloped, free-draining site rather than a low or heavy-soil border. As with other dieramas, established clumps resent root disturbance, so choose a permanent planting site and allow several years for plants to reach flowering size from seed.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in full sun with reliably good drainage; this high-elevation species tolerates coastal wind and cool temperatures once established.

directions: Dierama reynoldsii hails from the higher-elevation grasslands of KwaZulu-Natal and bears wine-red, inch-long pendant flowers edged with pewter-laced white bracts on long, arching stems from early to late summer. It forms an upright, narrow-bladed clump of grasslike foliage and has a reputation for toughness, withstanding coastal winds and fairly low temperatures better than many other wandflowers as long as drainage is sharp. It suits containers, rockeries, and cottage garden borders where its swaying flower stems can be seen against open sky. Like all dieramas it resents being moved once settled, so site new plants where they can remain undisturbed for years.
